title: Do Americans Need a Visa for Japan? (2026 Entry Guide)
excerpt: US passport holders can visit Japan visa-free for up to 90 days. Here's exactly what you need to enter in 2026 — and the online forms you can skip.
content:
Good news for American travelers: if you hold a US passport, you do not need a visa to visit Japan for tourism. You can enter under Japan's visa-free arrangement and stay for up to 90 days as a Temporary Visitor. There's no application, no fee, and no embassy appointment.

Below is everything you actually need to know before you fly, plus the online forms you'll hear about and whether they're truly required in 2026.

The short answer

US citizens get visa-free entry to Japan as Temporary Visitors for stays of up to 90 days. This covers tourism, visiting friends and family, and most short business trips like meetings and conferences. You cannot work on this status. There is no charge for visa-free entry, so any website asking you to pay for a "Japan visa" or "eVisa" for a tourist trip is one to avoid.

What you need to enter Japan

A valid passport

Your US passport should be valid for the duration of your stay. Japan does not impose the six-month-beyond-departure rule that some countries use for US visa-free visitors, but passport rules are exactly the kind of thing worth confirming on the official US State Department Japan page close to your trip. If your passport is near expiration, renew it before you go.

Proof of onward travel

Immigration may ask to see a return or onward ticket showing you intend to leave within the visa-free window. In practice most travelers booked on a round-trip flight never get asked, but have your itinerary handy.

Visit Japan Web: optional, not required

You'll see a lot of talk about "Visit Japan Web" (vjw.digital.go.jp). As of 2026, this is an optional pre-registration system, not a mandatory entry requirement. It lets you fill out your immigration and customs declarations online ahead of time and receive a single QR code that speeds you through the airport. At Haneda, Narita, and Kansai, 2026 Joint Kiosks read that one QR for both immigration and customs.

If you'd rather not bother, you can still fill out the paper landing and customs cards on the plane the old-fashioned way. Either path works. And just like the visa itself, the official Visit Japan Web service is free — never pay a third-party site for the QR code.

What about a 2028 travel authorization?

There are reports that Japan plans to introduce a digital travel authorization for visa-exempt travelers around 2028, similar to the US ESTA. As of 2026 this is not active — there is no ETA you need to apply for. It's worth a quick re-check on the official source close to your departure if you're reading this later, since entry rules are the detail most likely to change.

How long can you stay?

Up to 90 days per visit on visa-free Temporary Visitor status. If you need longer, or you're traveling for work or study, that's a different visa category and you'll want to contact a Japanese consulate well in advance.

Sites to avoid

Because visa-free entry and Visit Japan Web are both free, the main scam to watch for is unofficial sites charging a "processing fee" for either one. Go straight to the official government domains and ignore the rest.

Bottom line

For a typical American vacation to Japan, your to-do list is short: a valid passport, a return ticket, and — if you want a faster airport experience — an optional Visit Japan Web QR code. No visa, no fee, no waiting on an approval. Once that's sorted, the next thing to plan is your flight over.

title: Flights to Japan from the US: Routes, Times & Booking Tips
excerpt: Nonstop flights connect major US hubs to Tokyo and Osaka. Here are the routes, flight times from each coast, and how to find a good fare.
content:
Getting to Japan from the US is more straightforward than the distance suggests. Multiple nonstop routes connect major American hubs to Tokyo and Osaka, and the flight is long but manageable — most of it overnight or sleep-friendly if you plan it right.

Which airports you'll fly into

Japan has three main international gateways for US travelers: Tokyo Haneda (HND), Tokyo Narita (NRT), and Osaka Kansai (KIX). Haneda sits much closer to central Tokyo than Narita, so if you're starting in Tokyo and have a choice, Haneda usually saves you time and money on the airport transfer. Kansai is the natural choice if you're starting your trip in Kyoto or Osaka.

Nonstop routes from the US

You can fly nonstop to Japan from a wide range of US cities, including Los Angeles, San Francisco, Seattle, Chicago, New York/Newark, Dallas, and Washington Dulles. The two Japanese carriers, Japan Airlines (JAL) and ANA, both fly these routes alongside the major US airlines, so there's usually solid competition on price and schedule.

How long is the flight?

Flight time depends heavily on which coast you leave from:

  • West Coast (LAX, SFO, SEA): roughly 11–12 hours nonstop.
  • East Coast (JFK/EWR, IAD): roughly 13–14 hours nonstop.

Returning to the US is often a bit longer because of headwinds. Either way, build in a buffer day at the start of your trip to shake off the jet lag — Japan is well ahead of every US time zone.

What flights cost

Fares to Japan swing a lot by season, route, and how far ahead you book. Cherry blossom season and the fall foliage months tend to be the most expensive and the most competitive, so they reward booking early. Rather than quote a number that goes stale, it's best to compare live fares across dates — a flexible-date search will quickly show you which travel weeks are cheapest.

This is a good place to run a quick flight search and watch a few dates before committing.

Booking tips

Be flexible on your gateway

If you're not locked into Tokyo, pricing Haneda, Narita, and Kansai separately can surface a meaningfully cheaper fare. You can even fly into one and out of the other (an "open-jaw" ticket) — handy if your itinerary runs Tokyo to Kyoto, since you can depart from Kansai instead of backtracking.

Watch the peak windows

Aim to book well ahead for late March–April and October–November. Avoid Japan's domestic holiday crunches like Golden Week if you can, since they spike both airfare and crowds.

Consider the arrival time

An afternoon or evening arrival makes it easier to head straight to your hotel and sleep, which helps reset your body clock.

Bottom line

Nonstop service from both US coasts makes Japan an easy long-haul to plan. Pick your gateway based on where your trip begins, search flexible dates to catch a good fare, and give yourself an easy first day on the ground. Once your flights are set, the next question most travelers ask is whether Japan is safe — and the answer is reassuring.

title: Is Japan Safe for American Travelers?
excerpt: Japan is one of the safest countries you can visit. Here's what the US government advisory says, the real risks to know, and the emergency numbers to save.
content:
Japan is one of the safest countries an American can travel to. Crime against tourists is rare, the streets feel calm even late at night, and the bigger things to prepare for are environmental — earthquakes and typhoons — rather than personal safety. Here's an honest rundown.

What the US government says

The US State Department rates Japan at Level 1 — Exercise Normal Precautions, its lowest advisory level. That's the same category as most of Western Europe. You can read the current notice on the State Department Japan advisory page, which is worth a glance before any trip.

The real risks: nature, not crime

Japan is a very low-crime country, so the main risks are environmental. The country sits in an active seismic zone, so earthquakes happen, and the late-summer months bring typhoon season. Neither should put you off — Japan is extraordinarily well prepared, with some of the best building codes and warning systems in the world — but it's smart to know the basics:

  • Save the official disaster-alert apps and know that hotels post evacuation guidance.
  • If you travel in August, watch the forecast for typhoons, which can disrupt flights and trains.
  • In an earthquake, follow local guidance — drop, cover, and hold on indoors.

Crime and scams

Violent crime against tourists is very rare. The few issues that do come up are concentrated in nightlife districts: occasional bar or taxi overcharging in areas like Kabukicho and Roppongi, and the odd fake "tour guide" near major stations. The fix is simple — use metered taxis, be cautious about strangers steering you into a specific bar, and stick to reputable venues at night.

Health and water

No vaccines are required to enter Japan. The CDC recommends being up to date on routine vaccinations like MMR, Hepatitis A and B, and the flu shot — the same advice for most destinations. Tap water is safe to drink throughout Japan, so you can refill a bottle anywhere.

Japan's medical care is excellent but can be expensive for visitors, and you'll be paying out of pocket without coverage. Travel insurance that includes medical and trip disruption is worth pricing out before you go, especially given how much a long-haul trip costs to begin with — this is a sensible spot to compare a plan.

Emergency numbers to save

  • Police: 110
  • Ambulance / Fire: 119
  • US Embassy, Tokyo: +81-3-3224-5000

Bottom line

For an American traveler, Japan ranks among the easiest and safest places to visit. Take normal precautions, keep an eye on the weather if you go in typhoon season, save the emergency numbers, and consider travel insurance for peace of mind. With safety squared away, the next practical question is how to handle money on the ground.

title: Money in Japan: Cash, Cards & IC Cards Explained
excerpt: Japan is more cash-friendly than the US. Here's how to pay, where US cards work, which ATMs to use, and why you don't tip.
content:
Money in Japan trips up a lot of first-time American visitors, because the country is more cash-oriented than the US — even though it feels ultra-modern in every other way. Here's how to pay for things smoothly.

Cash still matters

Credit cards are widely accepted in cities, hotels, department stores, and tourist spots. But plenty of small restaurants, neighborhood shops, temples, and rural businesses still take cash only. The rule of thumb: carry more yen than you think you'll need, especially once you leave the big cities. Japan is very safe, so carrying cash isn't a worry the way it might be elsewhere.

The currency

Japan uses the Japanese yen (¥). Exchange rates move constantly, so check the current USD-to-yen rate close to your trip rather than relying on an old figure. A quick mental conversion at the rate of the day will save you from sticker shock or overspending.

Getting yen: use the right ATMs

The easiest way to get cash is withdrawing from an ATM with your US debit card once you arrive — the rate is usually better than airport currency desks. The catch is that not every Japanese ATM accepts foreign cards. The reliable ones are:

  • 7-Eleven ATMs (in their convenience stores, which are everywhere)
  • Japan Post Bank ATMs (at post offices)

Both consistently accept foreign cards and have English menus. Tell your bank you're traveling so they don't freeze the card.

IC cards: your transit lifeline

This is the one piece of "money" advice that matters most day to day. An IC card — Suica or Pasmo — is a rechargeable tap card you'll use constantly for trains, subways, and buses, and you can also tap it to pay at convenience stores, vending machines, and many shops. Load it with cash at any station machine and tap in and out. It turns the transit system from confusing to effortless. Get one as soon as you land.

Tipping: don't

Here's the big cultural shift for Americans: there is no tipping in Japan. Service is already included, and leaving extra cash can actually cause confusion or be politely refused. This applies to restaurants, taxis, and hotels alike. Don't tip — it's not rude, it's simply not the custom.

How much money to budget

Daily costs vary widely depending on your travel style — from budget travelers eating at convenience stores and ramen counters, to mid-range travelers staying in business hotels, to higher-end stays in ryokan with kaiseki dinners. Because prices and exchange rates shift, it's best to price your specific hotels and meals at current rates rather than lock in a daily number. Convenience-store meals and standing ramen shops keep food costs low; rail and nice hotels are where budgets climb.

Customs note

If you're carrying very large sums, be aware Japan requires you to declare amounts over the equivalent of about ¥1,000,000 at customs. Most travelers never come close.

Bottom line

Carry cash, get a Suica or Pasmo on arrival, use 7-Eleven or Japan Post ATMs for withdrawals, and forget everything you know about tipping. Sort that out and the money side of your trip basically runs itself — leaving you free to think about when to go.

title: Japan Etiquette: 10 Things Americans Should Know
excerpt: A few simple customs go a long way in Japan. Here are the etiquette basics every American traveler should know before arriving.
content:
Japanese etiquette can feel intimidating from afar, but the essentials are simple, and locals are gracious with visitors who make an effort. None of this requires memorizing a rulebook — just absorbing a handful of habits that differ from American norms. Here are the ones that matter most.

1. Don't tip

This is the big one for Americans. Tipping isn't customary anywhere in Japan — not in restaurants, taxis, or hotels. Service is included, and leaving extra can cause confusion. Skip it entirely.

2. Don't eat while walking

Eating on the go is generally frowned upon. If you buy street food or a snack, it's polite to stand near the stall or step aside and finish it there rather than wandering down the street eating.

3. Be quiet on public transit

Trains and subways are notably hushed. Keep phone calls off, set your phone to silent, and keep conversations low. It's one of the most noticeable cultural differences and easy to honor.

4. Queue properly

Japan runs on orderly lines — for trains, elevators, shops, everything. Look for the floor markings on train platforms and line up where indicated. Cutting is a real faux pas.

5. Take your shoes off indoors

Remove your shoes when entering homes, traditional ryokan inns, some restaurants, and temple buildings. Watch for a step up, a shoe rack, or slippers laid out — those are your cue.

6. Dress respectfully at temples and shrines

There's no strict dress code in Japan generally, but at temples and shrines lean conservative — covered shoulders and avoiding very revealing clothing shows respect at sacred sites.

7. Handle cards and money with both hands

When paying, you'll often see a small tray for your cash or card rather than handing it directly. Using both hands to give and receive cards, money, or business cards is a sign of politeness.

8. Bow when greeting

A slight bow is the standard greeting and a sign of thanks or respect. You don't need to get the angles perfect — a small, sincere nod is warmly received from a visitor.

9. Carry your trash

Public trash cans are surprisingly rare. The norm is to carry your garbage with you until you find a bin or get back to your hotel. Pack a small bag for wrappers and bottles.

10. Mind the small courtesies

Don't blow your nose loudly in public, don't point at people, and when in doubt, observe what those around you are doing and follow suit. A little attentiveness goes a long way.

Bottom line

None of this is hard, and locals genuinely appreciate the effort. Master these ten habits and you'll move through Japan comfortably and respectfully. With the cultural basics down, the last piece of practical prep is figuring out how to get around.
